concept.name: Fixed-income arbitrage
concept.definition: A group of market-neutral strategies that exploit pricing differences between related fixed-income securities or contracts, such as swap-spread, yield-curve, mortgage, and cash-futures basis trades. Positions pair long and short exposures in economically similar instruments and bet on the convergence of small yield or price discrepancies, usually with substantial leverage.
concept.intuition: Two bonds or rates that should be priced almost identically sometimes are not; fixed-income arbs buy the cheap one, short the rich one, and wait for the tiny gap to close.
concept.mechanics: Traders identify rich/cheap points using yield-curve models, financing via repo; typical trades include long Treasury/short swap (swap-spread), butterfly structures on the curve, long MBS hedged with Treasuries or swaps, and long cash bond/short futures (basis). Returns per trade are small, so leverage is high.
concept.formula: Swap spread = yield to maturity of the Treasury bond minus the fixed rate of the matched-maturity interest-rate swap (sign conventions vary by market).
concept.failure_modes: High leverage on small spreads means liquidity and financing shocks force losses: the LTCM collapse (1998) and the March 2020 Treasury basis unwind show convergence trades diverging further before converging, triggering margin spirals.
concept.misconceptions: That convergence is guaranteed within a tolerable horizon; 'riskless' relative-value trades can stay mispriced longer than a levered trader can stay solvent.
concept.example: A desk buys the cheapest-to-deliver 10-year Treasury, shorts the matched futures contract, finances the bond in repo, and plans to hold the position as the basis converges toward delivery.

citations.source: OFR Brief 20-01: Basis Trades and Treasury Market Illiquidity
